complexity_detail.description: Function literal `func Signature FunctionBody` denotes an anonymous function value.
Short variable declaration `a := expr` declares and initializes a new variable.
A variable declared with an initializer and no type takes the TYPE of the initialization value, which depends on the surrounding expression rather than on the declaration form.
A slice type `[]T` is a descriptor for a contiguous segment of an underlying array; its length may change during execution.
A slice composite literal `[]T{...}` creates a new underlying array and a slice of the whole array.
Index expression `a[x]` on a slice yields the element at index x.
An out-of-range slice index causes a run-time panic; whether the index is in range is not a property of the index expression itself.

`return expr` terminates the enclosing function and supplies its result.
`int` is a predeclared signed integer type whose size is implementation-specific (32 or 64 bits).

Remainder `%` satisfies x = q*y + r with |r| < |y|, so it takes the sign of the dividend.
The normal truncated-division rule has one carve-out: for the most negative dividend, x / -1 == x and r == 0 due to two's-complement overflow.

F-1: (1) `sort.Sort(sort.Reverse(sort.IntSlice(xs)))` orders `xs` descending using Go's standard ordering facility and supplies the descending order EXPLICITLY, in the form that facility takes - a NAMED REVERSE-ORDERING OPERATION, which the task lists as an admissible explicit form. The fragment does not rely on the facility's default order: sort.Sort is documented to sort 'in ascending order as determined by the Less method', and sort.Reverse 'returns the reverse order for data', so the order actually used is written at the site. (2) `lt := a < b` binds the strict-less-than result of the ordinary comparison operator. Exactly two statements. F-2/F-3/F-4: standard library only (package sort ships with the frozen toolchain), builds and runs under the frozen recipe, printing '[3 2 1] true'. gofmt-clean, go vet clean. F-6: the sort package carries no normative prohibition on Sort, Reverse or IntSlice. sort.Sort's documentation does carry the sentence 'Note: in many situations, the newer slices.SortFunc function is more ergonomic and runs faster', which is a performance and ergonomics note, NOT one of F-6's observable normative forms ('deprecated', 'should not be used', 'do not use', 'must not be used', 'unstable', 'internal', 'no compatibility guarantee'); the criterion is therefore satisfied. The sentence is quoted here as F-6 requires. R10 SELECTION RECORD (frozen tokenizer): `sort.Sort(sort.Reverse(sort.IntSlice(xs)))` + `lt := a < b` = 21 tokens [CHOSEN]; `slices.SortFunc(xs, func(x, y int) int { return cmp.Compare(y, x) })` + the comparison = 31 tokens; `sort.Slice(xs, func(i, j int) bool { return xs[i] > xs[j] })` + the comparison = 32 tokens. A 17-token form, `slices.Sort(xs)` then `slices.Reverse(xs)`, is REJECTED under R1 on two independent grounds: it is three statements where the task fixes two, and it RELIES on the facility's default order and then reverses the result, which the task forbids.

determinacy_enumeration: AUDIT CORRECTION 2026-09-18 (cross-language consistency audit). The pre-correction record recorded B=3 by collapsing int8/int16/int32/uint8/uint16/uint32 into one class and int64/uint64/int/uint into another, citing Rule 1.4.6, and by merging f32 widening with f64 identity into a third. Both merges are withdrawn. Rule 1.4.6 governs UNBOUNDED families (arbitrarily large overload sets, arbitrary user conversions, arbitrary trait impls, arbitrary macro expansions); six named primitive types are a bounded, enumerable set outside its scope. Rule 1.2.1 dimension 8 names signedness explicitly and dimension 4 separates 'whether a value is converted' from 'whether the conversion can change the value'. Quidra, whose float(i) accepts the same source set under the same no-overloading, no-implicit-promotion rules, split signed from unsigned as its classes 1/3 and 2/4 on exactly dimension 8 and reached B=6; Go faces an identical realizable space and must land on the same number. The RESULT type remains pinned to float64 in every class by the written conversion plus the identical-operand-type rule. CLASS 1 - `i` is a NARROW SIGNED integer type (int8/int16/int32): A5 = lossless widening, the conversion cannot change the value. Witness semantic-compression/witnesses/go/audit2026-09-18/f10p2_C1_int32.go (i int32 = 3): builds and prints 3.5.

CLASS 2 - `i` is a WIDE SIGNED integer type (int64/int), where values beyond 2^53 are not exactly representable: A5 = narrowing/lossy, the conversion CAN change the value. Witness semantic-compression/witnesses/go/audit2026-09-18/f10p2_C2_int64.go (i int64 = 9007199254740993): builds and prints 9.007199254740992e+15 - the written conversion silently lost the low bit.

CLASS 3 - `i` is a NARROW UNSIGNED integer type (uint8/uint16/uint32): A5 = lossless widening, A4 consumed = fixed-width UNSIGNED integer. Material against class 1 on dimension 8. Witness semantic-compression/witnesses/go/audit2026-09-18/f10p2_C3_uint32.go (i uint32 = 4294967295): builds and prints 4.2949672955e+09, exactly.

CLASS 4 - `i` is a WIDE UNSIGNED integer type (uint64/uint): A5 = narrowing/lossy, and the rounding is over a different value range than class 2's. Witness semantic-compression/witnesses/go/audit2026-09-18/f10p2_C4_uint64.go (i uint64 = 18446744073709551615): builds and prints 1.8446744073709552e+19.

CLASS 5 - `i` is float32: A5 = lossless WIDENING between two binary floating-point formats; a conversion is applied and the value's format changes. Witness semantic-compression/witnesses/go/audit2026-09-18/f10p2_C5_float32.go (i float32 = 3.5): builds and prints 4.

CLASS 6 - `i` is already float64: A5 = NONE (identity); no conversion is applied at all. Material against class 5 on dimension 4, which separates 'whether a value is converted' from 'whether the conversion can change the value'. Witness semantic-compression/witnesses/go/audit2026-09-18/f10p2_C6_identity.go (i float64 = 3.5): builds and prints 4. EXCLUDED CLASSES, carried over with citation and refutation (Rule 1.3.1.e): (a) A4 = fixed-width integer for the RESULT - NOT REALIZABLE, 'Operators' requires identical operand types and the left operand is pinned to float64 by the written conversion; mixing is rejected at compile time with 'mismatched types float64 and int32'. (b) A5 = an implicit promotion applied to the RIGHT operand - NOT REALIZABLE, flagged LOW-B-BY-ABSENCE: Go performs no implicit numeric conversion. (c) A1 = non-call/token substitution - NOT REALIZABLE, LOW-B-BY-ABSENCE. (d) shadowing of `float64`: NOT counted here, because the result type is also fixed by `d`'s external declaration and the classes a shadowed `float64` reaches are already the A5 classes above; recorded so the omission is deliberate, not silent.

complexity_detail.description: Assignability admits no implicit conversion between distinct non-constant numeric types - the rule that makes the written conversion mandatory and guarantees the other operand was not promoted.
Except for shifts, the operand types of a binary operation must be identical; an untyped constant operand is converted to the other's type.
Binary `+` is the arithmetic sum on numeric operands.
`float64` is the set of all IEEE-754 64-bit floating-point numbers, and floating-point arithmetic follows IEEE-754.
